notes.meaning: The Canaanite king of the city of Arad launched a surprise attack on Israel as they traveled through the southern desert. He took some Israelite prisoners in the fight. This sudden loss showed the people that they could not win on their own strength, but needed God's help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Excavations at Tell Arad show settlements from earlier and later times, but no evidence from the Late Bronze Age usually linked with Moses, leading some scholars to think ancient Arad was located at another site nearby.

notes.meaning: In response to the attack, Israel made a solemn promise to the Lord. They asked God to hand the Canaanites over to them, pledging to give up all the enemy cities completely to God. This meant they would destroy the cities and take no loot or prisoners for themselves.

The Lord answered Israel's prayer and delivered the Canaanites into their hands. The Israelites destroyed their cities and named the place Hormah, which means complete destruction. This victory reversed a defeat their parents had suffered in the same area years before.

Because Edom would not allow them through, the Israelites had to take a long, exhausting detour south toward the Red Sea. Walking away from the Promised Land through a rough and sandy desert worn out their patience. Their tiredness quickly turned into deep frustration with the journey.

The people openly complained against both God and Moses, asking why they were brought out of Egypt just to die in the wilderness. They grumbled about having no regular bread or water, and said they hated the manna. Despising the miraculous bread from heaven showed how ungrateful they had become.

The Lord sent poisonous snakes into the camp as a punishment for their rebellion. The snakes were called fiery because their bites caused a painful, burning sensation, and many Israelites were bitten and died. This harsh discipline showed the people how dangerous it is to reject God's care.

The deadly bites brought the people to their senses, and they went to Moses to confess their sin. They admitted that they had spoken wrongly against the Lord and against Moses, and they begged Moses to pray for the snakes to be taken away. Moses forgave them and prayed for their rescue right away.

The Lord told Moses to make a metal figure of a fiery snake and mount it on a high pole. God promised that anyone who was bitten and looked at the pole would stay alive. The healing would not come from the metal snake itself, but from trusting God's simple instruction.

Moses made a serpent out of bronze and put it up on a pole for the whole camp to see. Whenever a bitten person looked at the bronze snake, they lived. Jesus later taught that just as this snake was lifted up to save dying people, He would be lifted up on the cross so that everyone who believes in Him receives eternal life.

After the plague of snakes ended, the Israelites moved onward and camped at Oboth. The name Oboth means water skins, suggesting they were able to refill their supplies there. God continued to guide them faithfully toward their destination despite their weaknesses.

Israel traveled from Oboth and set up their camp at Iye-abarim in the desert east of Moab. This stop was along the eastern side of the mountains bordering Moab. They followed God's command to go around the edges of their distant relatives' land rather than attacking them.

Leaving Iye-abarim, the people journeyed north and camped in the valley of the Zered Brook. This stream formed the boundary between Edom and Moab. Crossing this valley marked the point where the older generation of doubters had completely passed away, clearing the way for the new generation to enter the land.

From the Zered, the Israelites moved across to the northern side of the Arnon River, camping in territory controlled by the Amorites. The Arnon was a deep canyon river that served as the border between Moab and the Amorites. God had forbidden Israel to take land from Moab, so they set up camp on the Amorite side.

An ancient collection of victory songs called the Book of the Wars of the Lord is quoted to show where the borders lay. The lines describe the ravines of the Arnon River running down to the city of Ar along Moab's frontier. This ancient quotation proved that the area Israel approached was Amorite land rather than Moabite territory.

The camp then moved to Beer, a name that means a well. At this place the Lord told Moses to gather the people together so He could give them water without them having to ask. God kindly provided for their thirst before anyone even began to complain.

Israel was filled with joy and sang a song calling for the well to bubble up with fresh water. The tribal leaders and nobles helped open the well, using their walking sticks and staffs of authority in the sand. When leaders and people worked together with faith, God poured out His blessing.

From the well at Beer, the people marched through Mattanah, Nahaliel, and Bamoth until they reached the valley near Mount Pisgah. This high ridge looked out over the barren plains leading down toward the Jordan River. Israel had now arrived right on the doorstep of the Promised Land.

Israel sent messengers to Sihon, the king of the Amorites, asking for permission to walk peacefully through his territory. They promised to stay on the main highway and not touch any fields, vineyards, or private wells. This polite request showed that Israel wanted peace, not an unprovoked war.

King Sihon refused to grant Israel passage and gathered his entire army to attack them at Jahaz. Instead of simply guarding his border, he marched out into the desert to destroy God's people. His refusal and aggressive attack brought God's judgment down upon his own head.

Israel struck down Sihon's army in battle and took possession of his entire country between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers. They stopped their advance at the border of Ammon because it was fortified and God had forbidden them to take Ammonite territory. God gave His people their first major territorial victory.

Israel captured all the Amorite towns and moved into them, making their home in the capital city of Heshbon and the surrounding villages. This captured region would later be given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad. The victory showed the new generation that God was able to give them the homes He had promised.

Heshbon was King Sihon's capital, which he had previously captured from an earlier king of Moab. This historical note explains why Israel was allowed to keep the land. They were taking land from the Amorites who had seized it, not from the Moabites whom God told them to leave alone.

Local poets had composed a victory song celebrating Sihon's defeat of Moab and the rebuilding of Heshbon. The poem compared Sihon's army to a sweeping fire that burned through the cities of Moab and destroyed their rulers along the Arnon. Israel quoted this old song to highlight how strong Sihon had been right before God helped them defeat him.

The song mocked Moab and its false god Chemosh for failing to save its own people. Chemosh could not prevent Moab's sons from becoming refugees or its daughters from being carried off as prisoners by King Sihon. It demonstrated that idols have no power to protect those who rely on them.

The concluding lines of the song celebrated the total overthrow of the Amorite cities from Heshbon all the way south to Dibon and Medeba. What the Amorites had once captured with pride was now broken and emptied by Israel's God. The mightiest human kingdoms cannot stand when God decides it is time for them to fall.

Israel settled down and lived in the conquered territory of the Amorites east of the Jordan River. This rich land gave them safety and fertile pastures for their herds. It served as a reassuring pledge that God would fulfill the rest of His promises across the river.

Moses sent scouts to explore the Amorite city of Jazer to plan its capture. Israel then took Jazer and all its outlying villages, driving out the remaining Amorites from the area. This move secured their northern flank so their camp would not be exposed to surprise attacks.

Israel next marched north toward Bashan, a fertile region famous for its oak forests and fine cattle. Og, the giant king of Bashan, brought his whole army out to confront them in battle at Edrei. Israel faced another frightening foe before they even crossed into Canaan.

The Lord told Moses not to be afraid of King Og despite his great size and army. God promised that Og, his people, and his land were already handed over to Israel, just as Sihon had been. Believing God's promise gave the people courage to face terrifying odds.

Israel completely defeated King Og, killing him, his sons, and his whole army until no survivors remained. They took full possession of his land, gaining sixty fortified cities across the region of Bashan. These victories filled the new generation with faith as they prepared for the conquest of the Promised Land.
